title: Buddha
notes: Cited for: the Buddha's traditional life (Lumbini, Four Signs, leaving home at 29, six years of austerity, 45 years of teaching, death at about 80); scholars accept his historical existence; death about 480 BCE or up to a century later; the first sermon at Sarnath, the middle way, the first monks and the order of nuns.

title: Lumbini
notes: Cited for: Lumbini as the traditional birthplace; Ashoka's inscription shows the tradition existed by the 3rd century BCE.

title: Bodh Gaya
notes: Cited for: Bodh Gaya in Bihar, where the Buddha attained enlightenment under the pipal (Bo) tree.

title: Four Noble Truths
notes: Cited for: the four truths (dukkha, craving, cessation as nirvana, the Eightfold Path) and the meaning of dukkha.

title: Eightfold Path
notes: Cited for: the eight parts of the path and the three trainings of wisdom, ethics and concentration.

title: Buddhism
notes: Cited for: samatha (calming) and vipassana (insight) meditation.

title: anatta
notes: Cited for: no-self; five changing factors; the three characteristics of existence.

title: nirvana
notes: Cited for: nirvana as "blowing out"; extinction of desire, hatred and ignorance; not a place; nirvana in life and final nirvana at death.

title: Triratna
notes: Cited for: the Three Jewels and the refuge formula.

title: sangha
notes: Cited for: the four groups of the sangha; the order depends on lay support.

title: Why Buddhist monks collect alms and visit households even in times of social distancing
notes: Cited for: Thomas Borchert (University of Vermont): Thai monks' dawn alms round, the monk's blessing and the giver's merit; monks do not farm and eat what is offered in their bowls.

title: Vesak
notes: Cited for: Vesak marks the Buddha's birth, enlightenment and death on the full moon of Vesakha; lay offerings and merit-making.

title: Theravada
notes: Cited for: "Way of the Elders"; predominant in Sri Lanka, Myanmar, Thailand, Cambodia and Laos; the Pali canon; the arhat ideal.

title: Mahayana
notes: Cited for: "Greater Vehicle"; arose around the beginning of the Common Era; predominant in China, Korea, Japan and Vietnam; the bodhisattva ideal.

title: Vajrayana
notes: Cited for: "Thunderbolt" or "Diamond Vehicle"; developed in India and neighboring lands, notably Tibet; mantras and mandalas.

title: Guru Nanak
notes: Cited for: Nanak's birth in 1469 at Talwandi (Nankana Sahib), death in 1539; the river experience and "There is no Hindu; there is no Muslim"; his teachings; Kartarpur.

title: Guru (Sikhism)
notes: Cited for: sikh means "learner"; the ten Gurus, 1469 to 1708; Nanak naming a successor; authority passing to the scripture and the Panth.

title: langar
notes: Cited for: the langar serves vegetarian food to all; everyone sits in a straight line; it began as a protest against caste; it follows the hymns.

title: Adi Granth
notes: Cited for: compiled by Guru Arjan at Amritsar in 1604 with hymns of Gurus and Hindu and Muslim saints such as Kabir; 1,430 printed pages; hymns arranged by raga; opened each morning and put away at night.

title: gurdwara
notes: Cited for: "doorway to the Guru"; the scripture on a cot under a canopy; recitation and hymn singing; most have a langar; open to all.

title: Gobind Singh
notes: Cited for: Gobind Singh became Guru at nine in 1675 after the execution of Guru Tegh Bahadur; founded the Khalsa, a casteless order, in 1699; declared the Granth the Guru before his death in 1708.

title: Khalsa
notes: Cited for: founded on Baisakhi Day 1699 at Anandpur; initiation with amrit stirred with a double-edged sword; Singh and Kaur; the pledge against tobacco, alcohol and certain meats.

title: Five Ks
notes: Cited for: the five articles of faith of initiated Khalsa Sikhs and what each symbolizes.
